contract.standard: College-senior political economy, translated into language an intelligent high-school student can follow without already knowing economics.
contract.rule: Do not simplify the ideas. Simplify language, sequencing, examples, and definitions.

progress_impact.note: Primary lane remains Stage 4. Explorer earns zero completion points.

page_contract: Real human scenario (Arkansas when possible; ILLUSTRATION if fictional)
cell_six_layers: Why this tradition generally favors this

exemplars_this_pass.note: Vertical exemplar build. Freeze template after production review, then propagate.

learning_paths.label: 20 minutes
learning_paths.promise: I just want to understand the argument.

learning_paths.label: 1 day
learning_paths.promise: Give me a political economy crash course.

modern-market-capitalism.plain_english_opening: Modern market capitalism is how most large economies actually organize production today: private firms, markets, wages, finance, and government rules mixed together—not a pure textbook.

arkansas_scenario.label: ILLUSTRATION
arkansas_scenario.text: Imagine a poultry processing plant near a small Arkansas town. Farmers supply birds under contracts. Workers clock in. Trucks move product to national buyers. A bank holds loans. Shareholders (or a parent company) claim residual profit. Local restaurants buy some output. The county watches property taxes and road wear. That one plant already contains markets, ownership, labor, capital, power, and public rules.

modern-market-capitalism.technical_definition: A political-economic family in which privately owned firms generally allocate capital and labor through markets, with residual claims typically belonging to owners, while states enforce property/contracts and often regulate, tax, and stabilize.
modern-market-capitalism.mechanism: Prices and profits steer resources toward valued uses; losses push resources away. Ownership concentrates control and residual claims. Finance intermediates saving into investment. Competition disciplines—when it exists.
modern-market-capitalism.historical_origin: Commercial and industrial expansion from early modern Europe through corporate capitalism, Progressive regulation, postwar mixed economies, and later liberalization waves.

branches.name: Classical liberal
branches.idea: Rights, limited government, commerce under law

branches.name: Austrian
branches.idea: Knowledge and discovery through prices; skepticism of planning

branches.name: Chicago
branches.idea: Price theory, markets, and often deregulatory instincts

branches.name: Keynesian market economy
branches.idea: Markets plus demand management and stabilizers

branches.name: Ordoliberal / social-market
branches.idea: State protects competitive order and social balance

branches.name: Developmental
branches.idea: Strategic coordination to build national capability

branches.name: Neoliberal
branches.idea: Late-20th-century emphasis on liberalization, privatization, globalization

modern-market-capitalism.branches_note: Capitalism is a family of arguments. People inside it disagree fiercely.

thinkers_disagreement.title: Smith vs. Marx: Who benefits from production?
thinkers_disagreement.smith: Specialization and exchange can raise living standards; self-interest can serve others through competition—but concentrated merchant interests can capture the state.
thinkers_disagreement.marx: Ownership of productive capital structures class relationships; surplus tends to accumulate with capital owners; wage labor can mask unequal power.
thinkers_disagreement.question: They both observed industrial relationships. What did they see differently—coordination and growth, or exploitation and accumulation?
thinkers_disagreement.no_winner: Explorer does not crown a winner. It shows the disagreement.

six_questions.WHO PAYS?: Customers, workers (effort/time), taxpayers (rules, infrastructure, bailouts when they occur), and sometimes neighbors (externalities).
six_questions.WHO BENEFITS?: Consumers (when competition works), workers (wages), owners (profits/appreciation), communities (jobs/tax base)—unevenly.
six_questions.WHO OWNS?: Usually private owners, corporations, funds—sometimes heavily concentrated.
six_questions.WHO DECIDES?: Managers/boards under law and market pressure; politics shapes the field.
six_questions.WHO BEARS THE RISK?: Owners and creditors primarily; workers and places also absorb shutdown risk.
six_questions.WHERE DOES THE SURPLUS GO?: Owners decide among reinvestment, debt, wages, taxes, and distributions—subject to power and rules.

modern-market-capitalism.first_order: Firms produce; people get jobs and goods; owners seek profit.
second_order: Successful firms attract capital and scale
Housing and wages shift with local demand
Failures destroy local tax bases and careers
modern-market-capitalism.opportunity_cost: Capital used in one industry is not used in another. A subsidy to one plant costs the next-best public or private use of that money and attention.
modern-market-capitalism.strongest_for: No other system has matched market capitalism's long-run capacity to raise material living standards through innovation, specialization, and voluntary exchange—when competition and rules hold.
modern-market-capitalism.strongest_against: Market power, externalities, instability, and unequal starting assets can produce domination, insecurity, and compounding inequality without anyone needing to 'steal' in the ordinary sense.
modern-market-capitalism.empirical_note: Real countries are hybrids. Outcomes vary by institutions, not slogans.
modern-market-capitalism.scholarly_disagreement: Debates continue over how much inequality markets produce vs. policy; how much antitrust should do; how financialization changes incentives.
modern-market-capitalism.cc_position: Preserve competitive markets and private initiative; refuse to treat status-quo corporate power as natural law; measure household prosperity, extraction, and capture.
modern-market-capitalism.cc_uncertainty: Which Arkansas sectors clear honest public claims? How much concentration is efficiency vs. domination?
modern-market-capitalism.stage4_testing: Pass 4.1 already attacked COUNTABLE fantasies. Pass 4.3 will pressure behavioral/market reactions; 4.5 capture.
defend_other_side: Why might a reasonable person defend strong private ownership even amid inequality?
When could a merger lower consumer prices and still raise political-economy concern?
How can wage labor be both voluntary and unequal in bargaining power?
Why might bankruptcy be a feature rather than only a tragedy?
What would have to be true for laissez-faire to be insufficient in this Arkansas plant case?
modern-market-capitalism.argument_against_page: Public-choice and market-failure critiques: externalities, information asymmetry, monopsony, systemic risk, and captured regulation can make 'free markets' a misleading label.
modern-market-capitalism.what_evidence_would_settle: Market structure data, household incidence, entry barriers, and political-influence measures—case by case.

socialism.plain_english_opening: Socialism is a family of arguments that productive capital should be owned or controlled more socially—by workers, communities, or the public—so economic power is not permanently concentrated in private capital owners.

arkansas_scenario.label: ILLUSTRATION
arkansas_scenario.text: Return to the poultry plant. Under many socialist proposals, the decisive question is not only wages. It is who owns the plant, who sets investment, and who claims surplus after costs. A worker cooperative, a municipal enterprise, or a heavily socialized sector would answer differently than an investor-owned corporation.

socialism.technical_definition: A tradition seeking to socialize or democratize ownership/control of productive capital to varying degrees, aiming to reduce class domination arising from private capital concentration.
socialism.mechanism: If ownership of capital concentrates residual claims and workplace power, then changing ownership/control changes who directs investment and who receives surplus—trading some market-allocation features for social direction.
socialism.historical_origin: Industrial-era critiques of capital concentration and wage labor; 19th–20th century movements spanning reform, revolution, cooperatives, and state experiments.

branches.name: Marxist
branches.idea: Class analysis of capital; historical conflict over surplus

branches.name: Democratic socialist
branches.idea: Deepen social ownership through democratic politics

branches.name: Market socialist
branches.idea: Social ownership with market allocation in many goods

branches.name: Cooperative
branches.idea: Member ownership without necessarily abolishing markets

socialism.branches_note: If you leave this page thinking 'socialism means government controls everything,' the page failed.

thinkers_disagreement.title: Market socialists vs. planners: How should socialized capital allocate?
thinkers_disagreement.side_a: Some socialists keep markets for consumer goods while socializing ownership of major capital.
thinkers_disagreement.side_b: Others distrust markets as reproducing unequal power and prefer planning or democratic allocation.
thinkers_disagreement.question: Is the core problem private ownership, market allocation, or both?
thinkers_disagreement.no_winner: Internal socialist debate is as important as external critique.

six_questions.WHO PAYS?: Society via taxes, retained social surplus, or diverted private claims—depending on model.
six_questions.WHO BENEFITS?: Intended: broader public/workers; risk: political insiders if accountability fails.
six_questions.WHO OWNS?: Workers, communities, municipalities, or the state—by design.
six_questions.WHO DECIDES?: Democratic or administrative bodies; contested in practice.
six_questions.WHO BEARS THE RISK?: Often the public or worker-members collectively.
six_questions.WHERE DOES THE SURPLUS GO?: Toward social aims, reinvestment, or member shares—again by design.

second_order: Political contests move into economic management
Soft-budget risks appear if losses are socialized without discipline
socialism.opportunity_cost: Socializing a sector uses political capital and fiscal capacity that cannot simultaneously deepen other reforms.
socialism.strongest_for: Takes seriously that capital ownership can become domination; asks democracy to reach the economy, not stop at the ballot box.
socialism.strongest_against: Information, incentive, and political-concentration failure modes—especially when economic and political power fuse.
socialism.empirical_note: Historical state-socialist regimes are not identical to democratic socialist or cooperative programs. Do not flatten them.
socialism.scholarly_disagreement: Whether markets can be retained under social ownership; whether democracy can discipline large socialized firms.
socialism.cc_position: Agrees capital concentration can become domination (Extraction/Capture). Rejects social ownership as the default for every productive activity. Uses ownership-by-function.
socialism.cc_uncertainty: Where Arkansas essential systems fail private provision badly enough to justify public/social forms.
socialism.stage4_testing: 4.2 law; 4.5 capture/admin of public enterprise; 4.1 already refused fake public cash.
defend_other_side: Why might a reasonable person fear private capital power more than public bureaucracy?
How is a worker cooperative different from a ministry-run plant?
When could social ownership increase freedom rather than reduce it?
What problem is 'decommodification' trying to solve?
Why might market socialism still count as socialism?
socialism.argument_against_page: Austrian/public-choice critique: without residual private loss, calculation and discipline degrade; politics allocates favors.
socialism.what_evidence_would_settle: Performance of specific ownership forms on household outcomes, innovation, and political liberty—disaggregated, not sloganized.

social-democracy.plain_english_opening: Social democracy tries to keep mostly private enterprise and markets, then use taxes, regulation, and public services so people are not crushed by insecurity or extreme inequality.

arkansas_scenario.label: ILLUSTRATION
arkansas_scenario.text: The poultry plant stays privately owned. But workers may have stronger bargaining rules, unemployment insurance if hours vanish, public schools for their kids, and taxed profits helping fund roads and health access. The fight is over how large and how universal those buffers are—not usually over abolishing the plant's private title.

social-democracy.technical_definition: A reformist tradition combining market capitalism with extensive social insurance, public services, labor institutions, and progressive taxation—private ownership retained as the main productive form.
social-democracy.mechanism: Markets generate productivity; politics redistributes risk and opportunity through the social wage and regulation.
social-democracy.historical_origin: Labor and reform movements in industrial democracies; postwar European and Nordic models as touchstones (hybrids, not copies).

branches.name: Nordic social-democratic variants
branches.idea: High trust, universal services, competitive export sectors

branches.name: Continental welfare capitalism
branches.idea: Insurance and labor institutions with different family/work patterns

branches.name: Third Way / recalibrations
branches.idea: Later adaptations to globalization and fiscal pressure

social-democracy.branches_note: Not 'socialism' in the public-ownership sense—though critics on both sides blur the label.

thinkers_disagreement.title: How far can redistribution go before investment flees?
thinkers_disagreement.side_a: Large social states can coexist with competitive firms if institutions are credible.
thinkers_disagreement.side_b: High taxes and rigid labor rules can reduce dynamism and create insider/outsider divides.
thinkers_disagreement.question: Is the binding constraint fiscal capacity, politics, or globalization?
thinkers_disagreement.no_winner: Country evidence is mixed and institution-dependent.

six_questions.WHO PAYS?: Taxpayers and sometimes consumers via regulated prices.
six_questions.WHO BENEFITS?: Broad households via services and insurance—design determines inclusion.
six_questions.WHO BEARS THE RISK?: Shared: markets for enterprise risk; public for many life risks.
six_questions.WHERE DOES THE SURPLUS GO?: Owners keep most profits; taxes claim a share for the social wage.

social-democracy.first_order: Private production continues; public buffers expand.
second_order: Housing and wage incidence of transfers appear
social-democracy.opportunity_cost: Every universal program competes with tax relief, public investment, or deficit reduction.
social-democracy.strongest_for: Historically delivered broad middle-class security in several rich democracies without abolishing markets.
social-democracy.strongest_against: Can leave ownership/capture problems undertreated; fiscal and demographic stress; may accept too much residual capital power.
social-democracy.empirical_note: Outcomes depend on trust, administration, and open-economy niches—not transferable by slogan.
social-democracy.scholarly_disagreement: Whether social democracy is a stable endpoint or a temporary compromise.
social-democracy.cc_position: Neighbor on markets-plus-security. Adds ownership tests, COUNTABLE honesty, Capture Loop, Replacement Readiness.
social-democracy.cc_uncertainty: Which Arkansas social floors are fiscally and legally durable without fake revenue.
social-democracy.stage4_testing: 4.1 already stressed fiscal capacity; 4.2 law; 4.3 household behavior.
defend_other_side: Why might private ownership plus universal services be freer than socialized ownership?
When is a tax a freedom-enabler rather than only a burden?
How can a social democrat oppose both laissez-faire and state socialism?
What problem does unemployment insurance solve that charity does not?
Why might employers support some social insurance?
social-democracy.argument_against_page: Supply-side and public-choice critiques: work disincentives, bureaucratic expansion, and tax competition.
social-democracy.what_evidence_would_settle: Household security metrics, employment, fiscal sustainability, and mobility—over decades, not anecdotes.

constitutional-capitalism.plain_english_opening: Constitutional Capitalism asks how Arkansas can keep markets, ownership, and liberty while preventing concentrated economic power or concentrated government power from dominating citizens—and make household prosperity compound across generations.

arkansas_scenario.label: ILLUSTRATION
arkansas_scenario.text: Same poultry plant. CC does not begin with 'nationalize it' or 'deregulate everything.' It asks: Is the market competitive? Who owns surplus? Are household wages, prices, time, and health improving? Is political influence being purchased? If public money took risk, is there a defensible public claim—after costs, not before? If a tax is to be retired someday, what COUNTABLE replacement exists?

constitutional-capitalism.technical_definition: A constitutional political-economic architecture: competitive markets and broadening ownership under constitutional constraint, democratic accountability, and public-purpose discipline, with household prosperity as the unit of success and public income only after a waterfall to reserved cash.
constitutional-capitalism.mechanism: Join market discovery + ownership-by-function + Capture Loop breakers + Four Roles + Dependency Rule + household measurement. Refuse teleported COUNTABLE cash.
constitutional-capitalism.historical_origin: Not descended fully formed. Inherits and modifies liberal constitutionalism, market discovery, Progressive anti-domination instincts, social-insurance insights, ownership-breadth ideas, and developmental capability lessons—joined under Arkansas-specific constraint.
constitutional-capitalism.branches_note: CC is an architecture under test—not a claim that every pilot succeeds.

thinkers_disagreement.title: Keynes vs. Hayek (and why CC refuses to pick a mascot)
thinkers_disagreement.keynes: When aggregate demand collapses, waiting for markets alone can waste lives and capacity.
thinkers_disagreement.hayek: Knowledge is dispersed; political intervention can amplify error and concentrate power.
thinkers_disagreement.question: What did Depression, stagflation, 2008, and COVID each teach—and fail to settle?
thinkers_disagreement.no_winner: CC borrows stabilizers' concern for households and Hayekian respect for discovery—then adds capture and COUNTABLE discipline.

six_questions.WHO BENEFITS?: Must show household pathways, not only GSP.
six_questions.WHO OWNS?: Function, risk, capital source, public purpose.
six_questions.WHO BEARS THE RISK?: Aligned with residual claims; no silent public backstop without claim.
six_questions.WHERE DOES THE SURPLUS GO?: Follow ownership/risk; public share only after waterfall.

constitutional-capitalism.first_order: Build measurable systems around household prosperity.
second_order: Stage 4 will try to break remaining claims
constitutional-capitalism.opportunity_cost: Every public dollar and every political fight uses scarce attention. Stage 4.1 showed replacement capacity is not free.
constitutional-capitalism.strongest_for: Makes anti-domination constitutional and measurable; refuses fake fiscal precision.
constitutional-capitalism.strongest_against: May under-deliver mobilization narratives; unproven feeders; legal and administrative constraints may bind tightly.
constitutional-capitalism.empirical_note: Stage 3 certified completeness to test. Stage 4.1 kept COUNTABLE at $0.
constitutional-capitalism.scholarly_disagreement: Whether ownership-by-function can be operationalized without sliding into ad hoc politics.
constitutional-capitalism.cc_position: See Unabridged Is/Is Not and Master Map.
constitutional-capitalism.cc_uncertainty: Listed openly on Stage 4 boards—unknowns are features of honesty.
constitutional-capitalism.stage4_testing: 4.1 fiscal done; 4.2 legal next; then household/behavior, resilience, capture, red team.
defend_other_side: Why might a social democrat say CC underweights universal decommodification?
Why might a libertarian say Four Roles still trusts government too much?
Why might a socialist say ownership-by-function preserves capital domination?
Why might a developmental state advocate say CC is too slow?
What would falsify CC's household-prosperity test?
constitutional-capitalism.argument_against_page: If CC cannot produce COUNTABLE capacity, tax-transition rhetoric is aspirational politics. Pass 4.1 already marked near-term COUNTABLE > $0 as FAILED.
constitutional-capitalism.what_evidence_would_settle: Honest feeder clearance through the waterfall; legal pathways; household incidence; capture resistance under stress.

ownership.title: Ownership
ownership.question: Who should own things?
ownership.plain: Ownership is not just having your name on a thing. It is a bundle of rights: control, income, risk, transfer, and appreciation.
ownership.imagine: Two neighbors. One owns the kitchen equipment and building for a café. The other rents everything and keeps only wages. Same customers—different ten-year futures.
ownership.technical: A bundle of residual control and income rights over an asset, including alienation and liability—distinct from possession alone.
ownership.mechanism: Ownership assigns who decides and who receives what remains after obligations. That assignment shapes incentives, risk-taking, and political power when assets concentrate.
ownership.compounding_bridge: Income → surplus → assets → returns → more assets. Starting wealth changes trajectories even without theft.
schools: Capitalist: strong presumption for private productive ownership
ownership.arkansas: Family farmland, a Fort Smith manufacturer, a Little Rock rental, a rural co-op utility—each is ownership with different power implications.

six_questions.WHO PAYS?: Buyers of assets; taxpayers if public capital is used
six_questions.WHO BEARS THE RISK?: Usually residual claimants—unless losses are socialized

ownership.opportunity_cost: Public ownership of one asset uses fiscal and political capacity not available elsewhere.
ownership.for: Clear ownership enables investment and accountability for care of assets.
ownership.against: Concentrated ownership can dominate workers, consumers, and politics.
ownership.cc: Ask function, risk, capital source, competition, public purpose—see Ownership Spectrum.
ownership.stage4: 4.1 rejected default public ownership; incidence and geography still open.
defend: Explain why a cooperative is still private property.
Explain why a passive shareholder differs from an entrepreneur.
Explain a socialist critique without using the word 'greedy.'

markets.title: Markets
markets.question: Why do we even need markets?
markets.plain: Markets are systems where people buy and sell. Prices help signal scarcity and value so millions can coordinate without one planner assigning every tomato.
markets.imagine: Nobody sets a statewide tomato price each morning. Yet tomatoes appear in Arkansas stores. How?
markets.technical: Institutionalized voluntary exchange where relative prices convey information and ration goods under property rights and competition (when present).
markets.mechanism: High prices attract supply and discourage waste; low prices do the opposite. Competition disciplines power—when entry is real.
schools: Keynesian: markets can undershoot for long periods
Socialist critiques: markets encode unequal bargaining power
markets.arkansas: A farmers market, a poultry contract, and a rural hospital market are all 'markets' with different failure modes.

six_questions.WHERE DOES THE SURPLUS GO?: Gains from trade—split by bargaining power

markets.opportunity_cost: Using politics to override a price also overrides the information that price carried—sometimes wisely, sometimes not.
markets.for: Coordinates dispersed knowledge better than central assignment in many domains.
markets.against: Fails under monopoly, missing rights, externalities, public goods, and instability.
markets.cc: Competitive markets are information systems that need rules to remain markets.
defend: Explain a market failure without rejecting all markets.
Explain why a price ceiling can create shortages.

capital.title: Capital
capital.question: What is capital?
capital.plain: Capital is anything that helps us produce more in the future—a tractor, factory, software, skill, or ownership stake. Money can be capital when it buys those things.
capital.imagine: Maria has $1,000 after bills. She can spend it today, hide it, lend it, invest in someone else's firm, or buy equipment for her own. What happens next is the beginning of capital formation.
capital.technical: Produced means of production and claims on them (physical, financial, human, organizational), valued for their expected contribution to future output.
capital.mechanism: Surplus not consumed can become capital. Capital earns returns. Returns can become more capital. Starting points and access to credit shape paths.
capital.compounding: Income → Surplus → Assets → Return → More Assets → Compounding
capital.unequal_start: Household A starts with $500,000 in assets; Household B with $0. Even with identical work effort, trajectories diverge—without requiring theft. Rent extraction, discrimination, and capture can intensify the gap.
capital.arkansas: A rice farm's equipment, a Little Rock family's home equity, and a manufacturer's CNC machine are different capitals with different politics.
capital.opportunity_cost: Capital locked in a mall is not in a factory—or in household buffers.
capital.for: Capital deepening raises productivity and wages over long horizons when complementary institutions work.
capital.against: Capital ownership can dominate labor and politics; fake 'capital' accounting can hide extraction.
capital.cc: Intergenerational capital rule; household net wealth; refuse counting hypothetical funds as COUNTABLE.
capital.stage4: 4.1 kept COUNTABLE $0; transition capital costs acknowledged.
defend: Explain why a house can be both consumption and capital.
Explain human capital vs. a tractor.

profit.title: Profit
profit.question: What is profit, really?
profit.plain: Profit is what remains after costs—if anything remains. It can be a signal, a reward for risk, or monopoly rent. Those are not the same.
profit.imagine: An Arkansas furniture workshop sells a chair for $100. After wood, wages, rent, debt, and taxes, something may remain. Arguments begin there.
profit.technical: Accounting profit is revenue minus explicit costs. Economic profit subtracts opportunity cost. Rent is return above competitive necessity.
profit.mechanism: Positive expected profit attracts entry/capital; losses push exit. Market power can sustain profits without useful signals.
schools: Socialist: surplus often framed as appropriated value
CC: surplus follows ownership/risk; public share only after waterfall
profit.arkansas: Same $100 sale can feed a local owner, a co-op, a public residual, or a multinational parent—Follow the $100.

six_questions.WHO PAYS?: Customers (and sometimes workers via wage bargains)
six_questions.WHO BEARS THE RISK?: Those who lose when profit is negative

profit.opportunity_cost: Taxing profit changes the next-best investment comparison.
profit.for: Profit/loss is a ruthless feedback system when markets are competitive.
profit.against: Profit can measure extraction as easily as creation when competition fails.
profit.cc: Distinguish revenue → profit → distributable cash → public share → reserved cash → COUNTABLE.
profit.stage4: 4.1 attacked fake COUNTABLE promotions of profit-like claims.
defend: Explain profit vs. revenue to a friend.
Explain when high profit is a warning sign.
Explain why zero profit can still mean a healthy competitive market.

norway.title: Norway — Resource Wealth Institutions
norway.tagline: Markets + private enterprise + public resource claim + sovereign investment
norway.BEFORE: Pre-oil Norway: smaller open economy, social-democratic institutions forming, no petroleum windfall.
norway.PROBLEM: How to turn exhaustible oil wealth into lasting national capacity without binge spending or private capture alone.
norway.THEORY: Public resource ownership/claims + disciplined investment abroad can convert depletion into financial intergenerational capital.
norway.INTERVENTION: Licensing/tax regimes; state participation; evolution toward large Government Pension Fund Global; fiscal rules constraining oil-revenue use in the annual budget.
norway.SHORT_TERM: Revenue surged; political temptation to spend rose; institutions were built to contain that temptation.
norway.SECOND_ORDER_EFFECTS: Macro sterilization via foreign investment; domestic politics around the fiscal rule; state-linked energy company evolution (Statoil/Equinor).
norway.LONG_TERM: Large sovereign financial assets; high living standards; ongoing debate about oil dependence and climate transition.
norway.DISTRIBUTION: Broad social services and wages in a high-productivity economy—not a simple dividend-only story.
norway.INSTITUTIONS: Parliamentary democracy, trust, professional fund governance, public legitimacy of rules.
norway.COUNTERFACTUAL: Many oil producers spent windfalls domestically, suffered volatility, or saw elite capture (resource-curse literature).
norway.SCHOLARLY_DISPUTE: How much success is oil + policy vs. pre-existing state capacity/trust; how transferable fund rules are.
norway.ARKANSAS_LESSON: BORROW the idea of intergenerational treatment of exhaustible wealth and honest public claims on resource rents.
norway.NON_LESSON: Arkansas does not have Norway's petroleum economics, population scale, or institutional history. Copy-paste is intellectually dishonest.

CC.MODIFY: Public participation proportional to public resource/risk
CC.REJECT: Treating Arkansas as if it possessed Norway's petroleum structure
CC.QUESTION: What Arkansas assets, if any, have comparable rent characteristics?

six_questions.WHO PAYS?: Resource extractors via tax/license; ultimately resource scarcity
six_questions.WHO BENEFITS?: Present and future citizens via fund/fiscal rules—and energy firms
six_questions.WHO OWNS?: Public claim on resource rents; mixed enterprise forms
six_questions.WHERE DOES THE SURPLUS GO?: Into foreign assets and constrained budget flows

gilded-age-us.title: U.S. Gilded Age → Progressive Response
gilded-age-us.tagline: When successful capitalism stops producing competitive capitalism
gilded-age-us.BEFORE: Rapid industrialization; national markets; weak competition policy; enormous productivity gains alongside harsh urban/labor conditions.
gilded-age-us.PROBLEM: Trusts in rail, oil, steel, finance concentrated corporate power; politics and markets intertwined.
gilded-age-us.THEORY: Progressives believed public law could restore competition, restrain predation, and expand democratic capacity without abolishing private enterprise.
gilded-age-us.INTERVENTION: Antitrust statutes and cases; regulatory commissions; later Progressive Era reforms (varied by domain).
gilded-age-us.SHORT_TERM: Legal fights; some dissolutions/regulation; incomplete and contested enforcement.
gilded-age-us.SECOND_ORDER_EFFECTS: Corporate legal strategy adapted; national administrative capacity grew; debates over expertise vs. democracy.
gilded-age-us.LONG_TERM: Antitrust and regulation became permanent American institutions—cyclically enforced.
gilded-age-us.DISTRIBUTION: Consumers and workers sometimes gained; capital owners contested; many exclusions persisted.
gilded-age-us.COUNTERFACTUAL: Without Progressive tools, concentration might have entrenched further—or alternative radical paths might have grown.
gilded-age-us.SCHOLARLY_DISPUTE: How effective early antitrust was; whether regulation solved or redirected capture.
gilded-age-us.ARKANSAS_LESSON: Use Extraction Test and Capture Loop. Scale is not automatically virtue. Competition policy is a market-preserving institution.
gilded-age-us.NON_LESSON: Do not pretend 1890 New York finance is Northwest Arkansas retail—or that one statute ends domination forever.

CC.BORROW: Antitrust as countervailing public power to keep markets markets
CC.MODIFY: Pair with household metrics and ownership analysis
CC.REJECT: Nostalgia that markets were ever naturally self-keeping without rules
CC.QUESTION: When does Arkansas-facing concentration harm households vs. lower prices?

gilded-age-us.thinkers_note: Connects to Progressive political economy and to CC Capture Loop.

six_questions.WHO PAYS?: Workers, consumers, rivals squeezed by trusts
six_questions.WHO BENEFITS?: Trust owners and allied finance—sometimes consumers via scale
six_questions.WHO DECIDES?: Corporate boards + captured or weak public rules

layers.simple: Private individuals and organizations generally have the right to own businesses, land, machinery, financial assets, and other productive property—under capitalism's common presumption.
layers.means: Owning a bakery isn't just a name on a deed. Ownership bundles control, income, risk, transfer, and capital appreciation rights.
layers.why_capitalism: Decentralized decisions, investment incentives, risk-bearing, entrepreneurship, and information—owners watch because they can gain and lose.
layers.complicated: A bakery isn't Walmart. A public corporation isn't a family farm. A monopoly isn't a competitive firm. A passive shareholder isn't an entrepreneur. A worker cooperative is private property too.

competitors.socialist: Separating workers from productive ownership concentrates power and surplus.
competitors.distributist: Property should be widely spread among families, not concentrated in capitalists or the state.
competitors.social_democrat: Keep private ownership; redistribute and regulate around it.
competitors.libertarian: Strong property rights are central to liberty; beware political reassignment.

layers.cc_question: Who should own this particular productive asset given its function, risk, competitive environment, source of capital, and public purpose?—then apply the Ownership Test.

why-monopolies-form.title: Why do monopolies form?
why-monopolies-form.opening: Imagine your Arkansas town has four grocery stores.
steps: They compete on price, hours, and quality.
Prices might fall at first—consumers cheer.
Smaller competitors struggle; entry gets harder.
why-monopolies-form.question: Did consumers benefit or lose?

terms_introduced.plain: Bigger operations can sometimes produce more cheaply per unit.
Fewer firms control more of the market.
Obstacles that stop new competitors from challenging incumbents.
Ability to raise prices without losing all customers.
Power as a dominant buyer—e.g., over workers or suppliers.
Owning multiple stages of a supply chain.
Benefit consumers get when they pay less than what the good was worth to them.
Return above what competition would allow.

traditions.name: Laissez-faire leaning

jargon_library.plain: How much people change what they buy when the price changes.
jargon_library.example: Gas rises 10%. Do people drive 10% less immediately? Often no—they still must get to work. Short-run demand can be relatively inelastic.
jargon_library.why_care: A tax on something people cannot easily stop buying behaves differently from a tax on something easily avoided—this is the start of tax incidence.

jargon_library.plain: What you give up when you choose something—the next-best alternative use of money, land, labor, or attention.
jargon_library.example: A $500 million public project costs whatever else Arkansas could have done with that capital and political focus.
jargon_library.why_care: Every policy hides an unseen alternative.

jargon_library.plain: A cost or benefit that spills onto people who didn't choose the transaction.
jargon_library.example: A factory sells for $12 what costs $10 to make, but smoke imposes $5 of harm on neighbors. Who really paid?
jargon_library.why_care: Private profit can diverge from social cost.

jargon_library.plain: In this project: public cash that has cleared the full evidence waterfall to reserved public funds—not hoped-for revenue.
jargon_library.example: Pass 4.1 kept COUNTABLE at $0 after hostile fiscal attack.
jargon_library.why_care: Prevents fake precision in tax-transition politics.
